channel.description: Posts in the discussion thread "Redzone RedDB Archive Asynchronous Copy Vulnerability"

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
The Foundation and other anomalous organizations would likely have lots of technical documents laying about. Requisition forms for staplers, budget projections for the HVAC maintenance staff, leave of absence request procedures for clerical staff, etc. etc. Just because they would be expected to have those things, however, does not make them inherently interesting to read if you were to come up with approximations of them and put them up on the site.

I think TyGently was correct in the summation that this is just a straight-up technical document with a few buzzwords added in. And aside from a few very special individuals, technical documents are not generally read for pleasure.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
This covers the exact same anomaly as SCP-2234 and if there is additional information presented here that develops a narrative, I am afraid that is too subtle for me.

Except for Warm Milk and Ramen all of these entries suffer from the same problem: a strong buildup with no real payoff. The anomaly here is extremely competently described, but it isn't especially interesting. It appears to be annoying anomalous spam about anomalous things, and nothing more. If there is more, I missed it.

I am left feeling like a read a technical document for some work related reason, that at least didn't make me frustrated with the author's inability to communicate the necessary information, in other words entirely emotionally neutral; which is how I am inclined to vote.

That said, I think the format, as well as the general concept of anomalous information technology support has a lot of potential.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I was also confused as to who exactly was writing this, in-universe.

It's a secutity bulletin from Redzone Security. This is actually based on a standard software announcement procedure in real life. Most software companies have similar security bulletins when they discover something that may be vulnerable. I believe AJ based this particular one almost directly on the structure of Cisco's software bulletin system.

(AJ can and should correct me if I made any errors in this explanation, but I'm pretty sure I captured the gist)

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Not sure why you'd allow it unless AJMansfield can prove he contacted someone on the GoI Contest Team before posting.

What's the use of having GoI formats if anyone can make something entirely unrelated and slap the tag on it?

-1 for blatantly ignoring contest rules, until I see evidence otherwise.

Edit: I'll go one further. Regardless of its inclusion in this contest, if this has not been discussed with the Prometheus Labs GoI contest team, and a template/instruction has not been added to the Prometheus Labs hub by a member of that team by the end of the contest, I am going to remove the goi-format tag from the article once the contest ends. Currently this does not qualify for that tag.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
From the contest page:

Now, you might find that a GoI format isn't working for you, or feels restrictive for what you want to write, even if you're sure you want to write with that group. Plus, making a GoI format doesn't have to just be limited to an anomalous object. They can pertain to other groups, events, memos, task forces, etc.

So if you want to write the format with a different approach, or even in a different format, contact one of the GoI team members if they are still around and talk with them about your idea and see what they have to say or offer. If they approve of your format variation, go for it. If they don't… there's nothing stopping you, sure, but at least take their comments into consideration.

This is a sketchy case, and I really wish this would have been shown to me before posting, but as this is justified in-universe as being a version of Prometheus, I hesitantly allow it. Of course, AJMansfield needs to provide a template for this around the time the contest ends (same for anyone who posts a GOI Format that hasn't been done before).

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: Not a huge fan. It's mostly a purely technical piece of work, which could be mistaken for any non-anomaly-related document if it weren't for the occasional presence of words like "infohazard" and "memetic". The bit with the banner ads and animated adverts was pretty much the only time this approached entertaining for me, and that was the only bit. Maybe others are seeing something in this I'm not?

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I like it. The anomaly itself is unfortunately quite skimpy as far as narrative detail goes, but I especially like that a software glitch capable of altering the physical world and producing dangerous memes is just being used to spam ads.

I also get the impression that this P-labs successor actually got their shit together after taking a tighter focus, which is nice. On the downside, similar to the anomaly, it's not entirely clear what anomalous services they offer besides "we can do IT security against anomalous things." If they stick around, I'd like to see what kind of paratech they bring to the table.

+1 in any case
